question: In venture capital, why is trying to see every deal in the market a flawed sourcing metric?

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Trying to see every deal is flawed because venture returns follow a power law: a tiny handful of companies generate nearly all the profits, so what matters is not how much of the market you cover but whether you see, recognize, and win the few outliers. Coverage measures activity, not outcomes.

Several problems follow from this. Seeing a deal is not the same as getting access to it; the best founders choose their investors, and hot rounds are often filled through trusted networks before they are widely shopped, so the deals easiest to "see" tend to be adversely selected. Chasing total coverage also spreads a firm's limited attention thin, leaving less time for deep diligence, building conviction, and developing the reputation and relationships that actually persuade top founders to take your money. It adds noise too, making it harder to spot the signal, and encourages generalist shallowness over a focused thesis where a firm has real insight and an edge.

Better metrics ask whether you saw the eventual winners in your focus area, saw them early, and won the allocation when you wanted it.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Trying to see every deal mistakes top-of-funnel volume for genuine access in a market governed by an extreme power law. Because a tiny handful of outlier companies generate nearly all venture returns, tracking thousands of ordinary startups adds little value, while missing or losing a single generational company defines a fund. Moreover, the strongest founders rarely run broad fundraising processes; they raise quietly from small networks of trusted insiders. Optimizing for total market coverage therefore floods a firm with noise and adverse selection—widely shopped, lower-quality rounds—while surfacing the best opportunities only after they are already spoken for. Even when a coverage-driven firm spots an elite deal in time, venture capital is not like public equities: seeing a company gives you no right to invest when top rounds are fiercely oversubscribed. Worse, chasing universal coverage spreads partner attention thin across shallow, reactive screening, crowding out the deep thesis work, early relationship-building, and conviction required to actually pick and win the few outliers that matter.

noweb.answer:
Venture capital returns follow an extreme power law, where a tiny handful of outlier companies generate nearly all industry profits. Measuring sourcing success by total market coverage mistakes volume for quality and confuses seeing a deal with winning it. The strongest founders rarely run broad, open fundraising processes; their rounds are often preempted or shared quietly within trusted networks, meaning a firm chasing indiscriminate coverage mostly captures adversely selected deals. 

Furthermore, pursuing every pitch creates severe cognitive and operational drag. Partner attention is finite, and flooding the funnel with noise steals bandwidth from deep thesis development, high-conviction diligence, and building the founder relationships needed to secure competitive allocations. Ultimately, a fund can see ninety percent of the market and still miss every generational company in the remaining ten percent—or spot the winners and fail to earn a place on their cap tables. Effective sourcing prioritizes proprietary access and early conviction in outliers over exhaustive visibility into the average.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Trying to see every deal is a flawed sourcing metric because it measures how many deals you hear about, when venture returns depend on getting into a handful of outliers. Seeing a deal is not the same as winning it. The best companies are oversubscribed, and their founders pick their investors. Access therefore comes from reputation, relationships and the value you add, not from how wide your funnel is.

Chasing volume also brings adverse selection. Deals that are shopped widely are often the ones better-connected investors already passed on, while the strongest rounds tend to close quickly through trusted networks. Volume also spreads a partner's time and attention thin, so diligence gets shallower, conviction is harder to build, and you have less to offer founders.

Because one or two winners can return a whole fund, the useful questions are whether you saw the right companies early, before they were obvious, and whether you won allocation. Seeing many deals tends to produce many passes or average investments, so it is a vanity metric. Better measures are how early you reach the best companies, how often you win the deals you pursue, and how good your selection is.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Trying to see every deal in the market is a flawed sourcing metric because venture capital returns follow a power law where a tiny handful of outliers drive virtually all performance, making broad market coverage a poor proxy for investment quality. Optimizing for volume floods a firm’s pipeline with noise, stretching partner bandwidth thin and reducing the time available for deep diligence, thesis building, and supporting existing portfolio companies. Worse, chasing universal visibility often creates adverse selection: the most widely shopped deals are frequently not the best ones, while exceptional founders tend to raise quietly from a small circle of trusted investors they already want on their cap table. Seeing a deal is also meaningless if a firm lacks the conviction, domain expertise, or reputation to win the allocation. Ultimately, effective sourcing is not about maximizing coverage of the entire market, but about cultivating high-signal networks and strong brand positioning to reliably access, recognize, and win the rare companies that actually matter.
